html:
Venice at the centre is the chart's name for the period, roughly 1378 to 1498, when the Republic of Venice dominated Europe's trade with the eastern Mediterranean. In Fernand Braudel's history of capitalism, it is the first clear case of one city at the heart of a European world economy.

The start is the War of Chioggia (1378 to 1381), in which Venice beat its great rival Genoa in the lagoon itself. After it, Venice ran the trade with the Levant almost alone. Spices, pepper, silk and cotton from Alexandria, Beirut and the Black Sea came west on Venetian ships.

How it worked:

  • State owned galleys sailed in regular convoys, auctioned each year to merchant groups.
  • German merchants had to trade through a single house on the Grand Canal, the Fondaco dei Tedeschi, where Venice could tax and watch them.
  • Venetian coins and banks set standards for the trade around them.

Venice used its money to build a land empire in northern Italy and keep a strong navy against the Ottomans. The end date marks the arrival of Vasco da Gama at Calicut in 1498. The Portuguese sea route around Africa did not kill the Venetian spice trade at once, but the centre of European trade moved to the Atlantic and to Antwerp.
